study.title: DKIST unveils MHD-predicted sub-50 km photospheric vortices

cover.headline: A solar telescope has captured **spinning plasma vortices smaller than any model predicted** could be seen.

slides.title: The telescope gives scientists their first direct look at the tiny spinning vortices that theory says drive solar energy upward.
slides.body:
These spinning structures may transport energy and magnetic twist from the sun's surface into its outer atmosphere. Models predicted they exist at 50 to 100 km across, but no tool could see them.

DKIST's sharpness is 12.3 km. That opens a window into how the sun's smallest spinning flows behave.

slides.title: The team reports 201 vortex detections in 3.2 minutes, with a median diameter of 38.6 km.
slides.body:
Virtually all detections were smaller than 50 km, placing them in the regime that models predict but no one had observed. Median swirling period was 37.3 seconds.

There was no preference for one spin direction over the other. That fits theory: Coriolis force is too weak at these scales.

slides.title: Previous solar telescopes lacked the sharpness to confirm that vortices this small exist.
slides.body:
DKIST is a 4-meter telescope observing at 416 nanometers. It analyzed a bright patch on the sun's surface containing concentrated magnetic fields.

The observations cover a field of view of 4.92 by 4.13 megameters across 143 frames.

caveats: This is a preprint. It has not been peer reviewed, so no independent expert has checked the work yet.
This study found a pattern, not a cause. Something else could explain the link between vortex size and the magnetic environment.

source.abstract: Solar vortices are rotating plasma structures that play a key role in the transport of energy and magnetic helicity from the photosphere to the chromosphere and corona. While numerical simulations predict the existence of small-scale photospheric vortices with diameters of $50$--$100$ km, no direct observational evidence has been reported to date, primarily because of the limited spatial resolution of previous instrumentation. Here, we analyze high-resolution observations obtained with the 4-meter Daniel K. Inouye Solar Telescope (DKIST) at 416 nm, with a spatial resolution of 12.3 km. Using Fourier local correlation tracking and the swirling strength criterion ($λ_{\rm ci}$), we identify 201 vortex detections across a sequence of 143 reconstructed frames, spanning approximately 3.2 minutes, within a field of view of $4.92 \times 4.13$ Mm. The observations cover a photospheric plage region containing pore-like magnetic concentrations. The detected vortices have a median equivalent diameter of 38.6 km and a mean diameter of $39.5 \pm 3.3$ km. Virtually all detections are smaller than 50 km and therefore fall within the subgranular regime predicted by magnetohydrodynamic simulations but never previously observed. The median swirling period, $τ_{\rm ci}=37.3$ s, satisfies the $τ_{\rm ci}<100$ s criterion established by MURaM simulations. No statistically significant preference is found for prograde rotation (53.7\%) over retrograde rotation (46.3\%), consistent with the negligible influence of the Coriolis force at subgranular scales. These results demonstrate the unique capability of DKIST to resolve the population of photospheric convective vortices predicted by state-of-the-art magnetoconvection simulations, opening a new observational window into small-scale solar convective dynamics.
